newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian plan to identify growth industries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian plan to identify growth industries.

text.p: Malaysia's new industrial master plan to be announced this week will focus on high technology and increasing productivity to sustain its industrial growth into the next century, economists said.

The second 10-year industrial master plan, to be announced by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad in parliament on November 28, will also find ways of reducing import dependence by developing forward and backward linkages within industries.

"We are trying to achieve a more wholesome industrial development. Activity in each industry must include the development of all components in the value chain," said Muthi Samudram, senior research fellow at the state-sponsored Malaysian Institute of Economic Research.

"What this means is that in each industry there must exist capability right from design and development to product manufacturing and its marketing," said the economist, who advised the government on the industrial plan.
"The aim is to develop industries which are self-supporting in all aspects," the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) said in a statement last week.
This would be complemented by developing local support industries, similar to the development that has taken place in California's Silicon Valley, MITI said.

Economists say this was a logical step for Malaysia, which has transformed itself from an agricultural to an export-driven industrial economy in just over a decade and hopes to become a fully industrialised nation by 2020.

Under the previous plan, which focused on large investments and rapid industrialisation, Malaysia attracted substantial foreign capital and technology to maintain economic growth of over eight percent for the past nine years.

According to Lum Chee Soon, general manager of research at Phileo Allied Securities in Kuala Lumpur, while agriculture's share of the gross domestic product has dropped to 20 percent from 30 percent 15 years ago, the share of industry has grown to over 30 percent from 20 percent.
"It (Malaysia) has moved from import substitution to export substitution," he said.
But in the next phase of industrial development Malaysia faced an enormous task of reducing imports, particularly of industrial intermediates, and developing its own technology.
Its export-oriented manufacturing industries had grown largely on heavy investments by foreigners and continued to heavily depend on imports, the economists say.
"What the government wants industries to do is to move from mere assembly operations to full-scale manufacturing," said an economist with a research house in Singapore.
"The lack of adequate base in high technology areas in an international environment where every nation is looking to do the same makes the task difficult for Malaysia," he said.
Lum of Phileo Allied said Malaysia was fast losing its competitive advantage as a tight labour market and the resultant wage increases were driving up manufacturing costs.

He said the country did not have any edge technically or in size of investments in areas such as aerospace, biotechnology and microelectronics chosen by the government for growth in the five-year economic plan to 2000.
"I would like to see the master plan come up with the linkages that go with the growth industries and how they will develop. If not the plan will be just another bureaucratic exercise," Lum said.
